title: The second arrow
hookLine: the first arrow is pain; the second is our reaction to it (Samyutta Nikaya 36.6)
last: STAND NEXT TO IT AND LOOK.

lines: A BARE FOOT, A CHAIR LEG.
cards: A dark kitchen, a glass of water, no lights on. A bare foot meets the leg of a chair, hard. That's the first part, and it's sharp, and it's real.
Then the second part arrives, about half a second later. Who moved this chair. Why does this always happen to me.
Now the toe hurts, and so does the whole night. Often, what keeps us awake is the second part. A short teaching of the Buddha has a name for each of them.

teach.b: First, same pain, two people. In the Samyutta Nikaya there's a teaching called the Arrow. The Buddha says an untaught person and a trained disciple both feel things: pleasant, painful and neither.
Pain comes to both. The difference is what happens next. Touched by pain, the text says, the untaught person sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast and becomes distraught.
Second, one arrow, then another. It's like a man struck by an arrow, the Buddha says, and then by a second arrow right after it. Now he feels the pain of two.
The first is the pain in the body. The second is the pain the mind adds: the sorrowing, the lamenting, the beating of the breast.

teach.h: SOME SECOND ARROWS LOOK LIKE COMFORT.
teach.b: Third, some second arrows look like comfort. The text adds that the untaught person, touched by pain, goes looking for sense pleasure, because he knows no other way out of pain. So a second arrow isn't always a rant.
Sometimes it's the snack, the scroll, the drink, reached for so the first arrow doesn't have to be felt.
Fourth, the first one still hurts.
The trained disciple feels the first arrow and not the second: bodily pain, yes; the added layer, no. This isn't a promise of numbness. The toe still throbs.
What drops away is the extra wound we fire into ourselves. And this isn't the poisoned arrow from the parable back in year one: a different teaching, the same honesty about pain.

how: Buddhist teachers use the two arrows to describe how the mind adds suffering to pain, and meditators practice noticing bodily sensation directly while letting the added commentary pass.

o: one who feels the first arrow of pain but not the second
a student who memorized every one of the Buddha's talks
one who has trained the body to feel no pain at all

games.q: you're the trained disciple in the Buddha's teaching. pain arrives in your body. what happens?
o: you feel the bodily pain, but not the added sorrow
you feel the pain of two arrows
games.why: one arrow, not two: the disciple feels bodily pain without the second, mental wound.

practice: Wait for something slightly uncomfortable to show up, an itch, a stiff shoulder, a sound, a worry, and find the first arrow: just the plain sensation.
Then watch for the second, the commentary right behind it: ugh, not this, why now. Don't fight it; notice it as a second arrow, and come back to the first, which may be smaller than it seemed.

wordCard.voice: Trained disciple, the one who, struck by pain, feels only the first arrow and not the second one the mind adds. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: feeling, pleasant, painful or neither, the word the arrow teaching is built on.

carryVoice: Your line: skip the second arrow. The first one is real; the second one is extra. That's day seven hundred one.
